title: Rehoboam's Harsh Answer and the Kingdom Divided
summary: At Shechem the tribes of Israel, led by the returned exile Jeroboam, ask Solomon's son Rehoboam to lighten the heavy yoke his father laid on them. Rehoboam rejects the elders' advice to serve the people and follows his young companions, promising a heavier yoke and scorpions instead of whips. The northern tribes renounce the house of David, stone his labor chief, and Rehoboam flees to Jerusalem, left to rule only the cities of Judah.
story: Solomon's reign ended in splendor (chapter 9), but the cost of that splendor had been heavy labor and taxation, and now it comes due. This chapter is the great turning point of 2 Chronicles: the united kingdom of David and Solomon breaks apart. From here to the end of the book the Chronicler follows the kings of Judah, David's line in Jerusalem, and mentions the northern kingdom mainly when it affects Judah. Yet he never stops calling the northern tribes "Israel" or hoping for their return. Chapter 11 will show Rehoboam forbidden by a prophet to make war on his kinsmen.
historical:
The division of the kingdom is usually dated around 930 BC. The Chronicler follows 1 Kings 12:1-19 almost word for word. But he omits the background in 1 Kings 11: Solomon's idolatry, the adversaries God raised against him, and the prophet Ahijah's meeting with Jeroboam, in which Ahijah tore his cloak into twelve pieces and gave Jeroboam ten, announcing that God would give him ten tribes. Verse 15 refers to that prophecy as something the reader already knows, a clear sign that the Chronicler assumed his audience had the books of Kings.

Jeroboam, an Ephraimite official whom Solomon had put over the labor of the house of Joseph, had fled to Egypt after Ahijah's prophecy and found refuge with Shishak (Sheshonq I), the Pharaoh who would invade Judah a few years later (1 Kings 11:26-40; 2 Chronicles 12). Shechem, where the assembly met, was an ancient center of the northern tribes, where Joshua had renewed the covenant (Joshua 24). That Rehoboam had to go there to be accepted as king shows that the north's loyalty to the house of David was not automatic.
cultural:
Kingship in Israel had covenant dimensions. David had been made king over the northern tribes by a covenant with their elders at Hebron (2 Samuel 5:3), and the assembly at Shechem seems to have expected a similar negotiation: we will serve you if you lighten our burden. The elders' advice in verse 7 reflects the ancient Near Eastern ideal of the king as shepherd of his people, who wins loyalty by serving them.

The yoke was the wooden frame laid across the necks of oxen, a common image for the burden of labor and political subjection. Rehoboam's reply uses crude, boastful imagery. “My little finger is thicker than my father's waist” (verse 10) is a proverb of excess; some interpreters think "waist" (literally loins) carries a vulgar double meaning. The scorpions of verse 11 may be a kind of whip with barbed or weighted tips, or simply a vivid picture of painful punishment. The cry “To your tents, O Israel!” (verse 16) echoes the rebel Sheba's cry against David in 2 Samuel 20:1; it is a call to disband and go home, withdrawing allegiance.
literary: The chapter is a tightly told story built on repetition and contrast. The phrase “heavy yoke” and the verb "advise" recur throughout. Two groups of counselors are set side by side: the elders who served Solomon, who counsel service, and the young men who grew up with Rehoboam, who counsel harshness. The contrast is sharpened by the similar wording of the request and the reply. The narrator's comment in verse 15, that this turn of events was from God, sits at the center of the chapter's resolution and interprets everything before it. The chapter closes with the narrator's summary (verse 19), “to this day Israel has been in rebellion against the house of David”, a line taken over from Kings.

doctrines.note: Verse 15 says the turn of events was from God to fulfill his word through Ahijah. Rehoboam's foolish choice is fully his own, yet God works through it to accomplish his purposes. Scripture holds divine sovereignty and human responsibility together without explaining away either.
Rehoboam rejects the counsel of experience for the counsel of flattery. The chapter is a case study in the folly of Proverbs: the wise listen to advice, and the proud reject it to their ruin.
The division of the kingdom is the consequence of Solomon's sins, as 1 Kings 11 explains, and of Rehoboam's arrogance. Judgment in Scripture often works through the natural outcomes of human choices.

words.note: Ol, yoke. It appears seven times in the chapter. The yoke is the burden the people bear, and the whole dispute is whether the king will lighten or increase it. In the prophets, breaking the yoke becomes an image of liberation.

Etsah, counsel or advice. Rehoboam rejects the etsah of the elders (verses 8 and 13). The word is common in wisdom literature, where receiving good counsel is a mark of the wise (Proverbs 12:15). Rehoboam's reign begins with the failure of wisdom that his father had been famous for.

Nesibbah, a turn of events. This rare word, found only here in the Old Testament, names what happened as a turning brought about by God. The parallel in 1 Kings 12:15 uses a related word. It gives the Chronicler's reading of history: behind human decisions stands God's governing hand.

Cheleq, portion or share. The question “What portion do we have in David” (verse 16) is a formal renunciation: the northern tribes declare that they have no share in the Davidic kingdom. The word often refers to a share of inheritance or land.

christ: Rehoboam's harsh reply stands in sharp contrast to the words of the son of David who came later. The elders urged Rehoboam to be a servant to the people, and he refused. Jesus said that he came not to be served but to serve and to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45), and he invited the weary to take his yoke, because his yoke is easy and his burden light (Matthew 11:28-30). The comparison is thematic, not a prediction in this chapter, but it is fitting: the division of David's kingdom began with a king who increased the yoke, and the gospel presents the true son of David as the one who lifts it. The prophets also looked forward to a day when the divided kingdom would be one again under one shepherd, David's descendant (Ezekiel 37:15-24), and the New Testament sees that gathering beginning in Christ, who draws scattered people into one flock.

hard.q: If the division was from God, was Rehoboam to blame?
hard.a:
Verse 15 says the turn of events was from God, in order to fulfill his word through Ahijah. Readers ask whether this makes God the author of Rehoboam's folly or relieves Rehoboam of blame.

The Bible consistently affirms both that God governs history and that human beings are responsible for their choices. Rehoboam freely rejected wise counsel out of pride; the text presents that as his decision, and the consequences fall on him. At the same time, God had already announced that the kingdom would be divided because of Solomon's idolatry, and he worked through Rehoboam's pride to bring it about. Christian theologians have explained this in different ways. Some stress that God ordains all events while never being the author of sin; others stress God's foreknowledge and his use of human choices he permits rather than causes. The same pattern appears in the story of Joseph (Genesis 50:20) and in the crucifixion (Acts 2:23). The text doesn't resolve the philosophical question, but it refuses to let either truth cancel the other.

questions: The elders told Rehoboam that if he served the people, they would serve him forever. What does this suggest about the nature of good leadership?
Rehoboam chose advice from people who grew up with him and told him what he wanted to hear. Whose counsel do you seek, and why?
The Chronicler says God was at work even in Rehoboam's foolish choice. How does that affect the way you look at failures, your own or others'?
